The Social Planning Council continues to work on making a difference in Williams Lake and area through its poverty reduction strategy. At the latest regular city council meeting this month, Angelika Sellick presented an update on the Thrive Poverty Reduction Strategy and the work of the Poverty Reduction Working Group. The working group was formed in 2018 with the strategy that was endorsed by city council published in 2021 following extensive community consultation. “We all know the social planning council is in no way the only organization that is doing poverty reduction work in our community,” Sellick acknowledged, adding they recognize and celebrate the richness of organizations doing poverty reduction in their own communities without any direct connection to the Social Planning Council established in 1995. Through community consultation Sellick said the Social Planning Council has come to understand poverty as the condition in which people lack the resources, means, choices and opportunities to maintain self-sufficiency and a quality of life that supports basic needs, dignity and meaningful participation in the community. The Social Planning Council is a table that meets monthly to learn, share and collaborate on practical action and advocacy leading to increased community social well-being. Some organizations involved are the Salvation Army, Interior Health, Gibraltar Mine, the Foundry Cariboo Chilcotin, Women’s Contact Society, and WorkBC, in addition to representatives from city council. “Poverty is not the outcome of personal deficiencies or lack of will. It is the result of greater systemic failures,” Sellick said further noting poverty reduction work at the local level can contribute and lead to the ending of poverty at a global level. Conservatives costed platform relies on economic growth that beats all forecasts The B.C. Conservative Party released a fully costed platform on Sunday afternoon, projecting that under a Tory government, the deficit will fall from $13.7 billion this year to $10.8 billion by 2029, aided by the party’s forecast of spectacular 3.2 per cent economic growth. This assumes 2.5 per cent growth this year, 2.8 per cent next year, and 3.2 per cent in 2029 — growth levels far beyond most current economic forecasts. Ross Hickey, an associate professor of economics and management at UBC Okanagan, says this type of growth is unlikely. He gave a “cautiously optimistic” forecast of one per cent GDP growth per year for the next three years. The Bank of Canada projects national GDP growth at 0.7 per cent this year, 1.8 per cent next year, and 1.8 per cent the year after that. The Royal Bank of Canada projects B.C.’s economy to grow 0.8 per cent this year and 1.5 per cent next year. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says his party will achieve these higher levels by “supercharging” the economy. “We are predicting roughly one per cent more optimism in this province than the NDP,” Doerkson said Monday. “And frankly, I think it’s completely achievable.” But Doerkson fails to explain how some of his promises, such as ending Clean BC or reducing permitting times, will create the growth surge he promises. Hickey says words like “supercharge the economy” don’t say much, either. “There is a lot of rhetoric about what’s going to happen, that’s going to lead to growth, but it’s not a plan for how we’re going to get more growth,” he said. This type of growth would make B.C. a leader among advanced economies, which the International Monetary Fund projects will grow 2.1 per cent this year and 1.8 per cent next year, on average. He didn’t finish high school, but went as far as Grade 10, court heard, and worked in construction sometimes. St. Germain asked him about his past criminal record, including a 2003 conviction in Ontario for possession of property obtained by crime, for which he served seven months, as well as a 2009 Ontario conviction for failure to comply with a court order. 77c8b180d6e84857b530587c33cb2bf0.text: Kent Rumbles was sentenced to four years in prison for a Nov. 6, 2021 head-on crash on the Bruhn Bridge at Sicamous that killed a Kamloops Shaun Stacey Michael. An Alberta man sentenced to four years jail time for a fatal collision in Sicamous has lost his court appeal. The collision occurred on the evening of Nov. 6, 2021, on the Bruhn Bridge where police found two pickup trucks had crashed head-on while crossing. The sole occupant of the eastbound truck, Kent Gordon Rumbles, was transported to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The driver of the westbound truck, a 48-year-old Shaun Stacey Michael of Kamloops, died at the scene. Police determined Rumbles’ vehicle had crossed the centre line. He was later charged and convicted of dangerous operation of a conveyance causing death, impaired operation of a conveyance causing death, and operating a conveyance with 80 milligrams of alcohol or more in 100 millilitres of blood causing death. In March 2025, Rumbles was sentenced to four years in prison. Later that month he was granted bail, having filed a notice of appeal. An appeal hearing was held on June 25, 2026, and on Oct. 16 Justice Karen Horsman released her decision: appeal dismissed. On the morning of Nov. 6, Rumbles left his home in Thorsby, Alta., driving to his seasonal property at Mabel Lake where he planned to meet his wife and mother-in-law. Horsman noted that other than taking a coffee to go, Rumbles, an insulin-dependent diabetic, “did not eat before leaving his house and he did not pack food for the trip.” “En route, the appellant stopped for gas. At that time, he purchased alcohol: a six-pack of White Claw hard seltzers, two bottles of wine, and a 750 ml bottle of raspberry vodka,” wrote Horsman in her reason for judgement. “As he continued driving, the appellant said he began to feel flu-like symptoms. 9a7e489f7350a02bb405aa78dd4cd028.text: CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko gestures during a B.C. election campaign stop in Surrey at Organic Warehouse, at 7093 King George Blvd. in Newton, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Affordability was the focus of another B.C. election campaign stop in Surrey for CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko on Monday morning, Oct. 19. The Surrey South candidate was at a Newton grocery store to reveal party plans “to put money back in British Columbians’ pockets, saving a typical two-income family approximately $540 a year.” Promised are lower taxes, a rate-of-inflation cap on residential BC Hydro rate increases, 20,000 new $10-a-day child care spaces by 2030 and a new refundable BC Commuter Credit to give passengers 15 per cent back on monthly/annual transit passes and BC Ferries multi-trip fares. If elected, CentreBC would reverse the NDP’s 2026 increase to the lowest provincial personal income tax bracket, reducing the rate to 5.06 per cent effective Jan. 1, 2027. Also, the renter’s tax credit will be increased to $600 a year and indexed to inflation. An existing freeze on ICBC basic insurance rates would be maintained until spring 2027, and rates would then be kept at or below inflation through 2030. “Our plan addresses household financial pressures together,” Sturko said at a podium set up in the produce section at Organic Warehouse. “People are working hard and still struggling to afford the basics,” said Sturko. “CentreBC will implement practical measures that lower household expenses, make bills more predictable and leave working families with more money in their pockets.” Sturko was named leader of CentreBC on Sept. 22 and announced her candidacy in Surrey South three days later. Many of the party’s campaign events have been held in Surrey, a key battleground in the B.C. election. 7dfcd1cde264563097ae3852dc185b3b.text: **By Cariboo Gold Dance Band hosting Juno award winning saxophonist Nov. 14** The Cariboo Gold Dance Band asks you to join them on Nov. 14 for "Swing n' Sax" with internationally known and Juno award winning saxophonist Campbell Ryga. A big band in the Williams Lake might seem a bit unusual but the Cariboo Gold Dance Band (CGDB) has been playing together for over 42 years. This 14-piece band, comprised of skilled and dedicated local musicians, played its first dance in the spring of 1984 and has performed for a wide variety of occasions in the Cariboo and beyond ever since. Each year the band brings to the community a professional to work with the CGDB and then perform as a featured artist. This year the dance band will be hosting the triple Juno award recipient and internationally respected saxophone player, Campbell Ryga. Anyone who has enjoyed the music of Michael Bublé and his Grammy winning album, _Crazy Love_, would have heard Campbell’s skillful sax playing. He has also been featured on over 87 other jazz recordings, often as a leader. Most notably, Campbell Ryga is a founding member of the award-winning Hugh Fraser Quintet. British Columbia is full of international acclaimed jazz musicians and Campbell Ryga is no exception. He was born in 1961 in Edmonton but was raised in Summerland, and is the eldest son of renowned author and playwright George Ryga. When he was 18, Ryga moved to Vancouver to pursue advanced musical studies. He has since lived and worked in Vancouver, Toronto, and New York City, establishing an international reputation as both a band leader and creative jazz artist. Ryga is currently based in Kelowna, and serves as a clinician, adjudicator, arts juror and it is a natural fit for him to be the headline performer in the Cariboo Gold Dance Band’s upcoming concert on Saturday, Nov. 14. Initial reviews were positive for “Hometown Giants,” a six-episode television series about the Langley-based WHL team, with commenters praising the behind-the-scenes look at the WHL franchise, while at least one warned it might not be suitable for young viewers. It follows the 2025-26 season of the Giants, centered on the involvement of singer Michael Buble and “Property Brothers” TV show star Drew Scott as part-owners in the campaign “to restore a team that hasn’t won a championship since 2007,” to use the words of the press release announcing the series had begun airing on Oct. 16, exclusively on Amazon’s Prime Video. “With a new coach and General Manager leading the way, the series captures the bold front-office decisions, roster-shaping trades, and high-pressure moments that define a season on the edge,” the release said. Online reviews were positive, praising the show for its focus on the young players. Movieguide.org said it was “worth the watch” while advising episodes “feature frequent foul language and some mild violence when players fight on the ice. This is an engaging watch for hockey fans and newcomers to the sport, as well as teens and adults, but the youngest viewers should skip it.” Daniel Baptista on The Movie Podcast described it as a “distinctly Canadian underdog journey that reminds you what makes sports so special. Heartfelt and hopeful, Hometown Giants is the kind of story you can’t help but cheer for.” User reviews on Internet Movie Database gave it eight out 10. “The bit where they’re in the dressing room after a tough loss and you can just see how young these kids are hits you. aaa97331fdbc03d89fcd483973c5c804.text: OPINION: Community forests offer a practical path forward for B.C. | Williams Lake Tribune OPINION: Community forests offer a practical path forward for B.C. Field tour participants review an area affected by a 2022 wildfire, shown in pink on the map, on a tour with the Kaslo and District Community Forest. British Columbia’s (B.C.) forest sector is at a turning point. Communities are feeling the effects of sawmill and pulp mill closures, catastrophic wildfires, changing markets, and general uncertainty about the future. British Columbians are also asking how forests can support healthy ecosystems, sustainable local economies, reconciliation, public safety, recreation, and other community priorities. We believe community forestry offers a tested and proven way forward and should be on the minds of British Columbians and on the platforms of those running for office in the provincial election. Community forests put decisions about local forests closer to the people who understand those places and live with the outcomes. Through long-term community forest agreements, a range of local organizations—including municipalities, First Nations, community organizations, and partnerships—can manage nearby forests according to local values. And the good news? The community forest model is already working across B.C. There are 62 operating community forests, each shaped by their local landscape, economy, relationships, and priorities. More than half are held directly by First Nations or operated through partnerships involving First Nations, creating opportunities for shared stewardship, economic participation, and reconciliation. Each community forest is unique, but they share the same fundamental goals, including responsible local stewardship, economic benefits that remain in the community, and sustainable management for future generations. 2688859221752a8e410030367fa39bfc.text: The BC Conservatives have announced Pavneet Singh will run in the Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding in the 2026 provincial elecion. The BC Conservative candidate for Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream said he’s disappointed in the “sleazy attacks” made by OneBC towards him. OneBC posted court documents to Facebook on Oct. 16, regarding the indictment against Pavneet Singh in 2006. The charges were that of sexual assault, sexual touching of a person under 14 and unlawful confinement. The charges were stayed in 2008. Singh addressed the 20-year-old allegations on Facebook, stating his innocence, claiming mistaken identity in the situation and added that he has no criminal record. “In 2006, I was celebrating Canada Day in a public park. An incident with which I had nothing to do with occurred, and I was mistakenly accused of being involved,” Singh wrote. “I was falsely accused, and when the Crown prosecutor realized that, the charges were stayed.” A Crown-directed stay of proceedings in B.C. criminal court lasts for one year under section 579 of the Criminal Code, during which that time the Crown can restart the prosecution if new evidence is found. If the Crown does not restart the charges within that 12-month window, the stay becomes permanent and the matter is officially over. By general policy, the BC Prosecution Service does not provide public reasons for staying charges, except in very rare cases. “In Canada, one is presumed innocent until proven guilty – not the other way around, as my political opponents would seemingly prefer,” Singh’s social media post read. “I’m confident that British Columbians will see these despicable tactics by opponents for exactly what they are.” Black Press Media has reached out to Singh for comment and the story will be updated should comment be received. Singh is running against OneBC’s Alexandra Wright, BC NDP’s Binny Boparai and BC Green Party’s Carter Mochinski.

Mario Canseco of Research Co. regularly polls British Columbian voters to ask which issues they care most about. For the past three years, housing has led. This year, it is cost-of-living. A back-and-forth emerged as campaigns questioned each other’s math and whether spending or tax-cut promises are realistic. a5d350122194c0c0075f3197b96e2e6f.text: Sam Roberts Band, Owen Riegling to headline when the CPKC Holiday Train crosses B.C. | Williams Lake Tribune Sam Roberts Band, Owen Riegling to headline when the CPKC Holiday Train crosses B.C. Owen Riegling will be performing on the CPKC Holiday Train when it makes stops across the province. Sam Roberts Band will be performing on the CPKC Holiday Train when it makes stops across the province. Sam Roberts Band and Owen Riegling are this year’s performers on the CPKC Holiday Train as it makes its way across Alberta and British Columbia this December. This is the 28th year for the holiday event which sees two trains – one which travels a predominantly Canadian route and the other mostly in the U.S. – making stops in different communities to offer free concerts, and raise money and collect non-perishable food items for food banks across North America. Cars on each of the trains are lit up in brightly coloured Christmas-themed displays. The U.S. Holiday Train kicks off on Nov. 19, in Montreal, and will wind south through towns across the United States, before traveling north again into Saskatchewan, where it will make its final stop. The Canadian Holiday Train kicks off on Nov. 21 in Jackman, Maine, in the United States, and will make its way west, through Quebec, down to New York, back into Ontario, then Manitoba, and into Saskatchewan, and then Alberta and B.C. “We are so proud to be part of the CPKC Holiday Train once again,” said the Sam Roberts Band online, noting it has been eight years since they last performed on the Holiday Train. Or, as they put it, “last rode the rails and rocked the mountains with you all, and we are very excited to do it all over.” From Calgary to Banff in Alberta and then from Golden, all the way to the final stop in Port Coquitlam, the band will be playing 33 shows from Dec. 11 to 20.
